w: Modeled on Berlin's Olympiastadion and inaugurated in 1938, this stadium hosted the 1962 World Cup final - Brazil over Czechoslovakia. Then came 1973: after Pinochet's coup, the same stands and tunnels were turned into a mass detention and torture facility. Its history holds both, uncomfortably, in the one place.
s: World Cup final host, then a torture camp
_facts: architecture based on the Olympiastadion in Berlin, inaugurated 3 December 1938
hosted the 1962 FIFA World Cup final where Brazil defeated Czechoslovakia 3-1
used as a mass imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial execution facility by the Pinochet dictatorship following the 1973 military coup

n: Chilean National Museum of Natural History
w: One of only three national museums in Chile, founded in 1830 by the French naturalist Claudio Gay, who spent years cataloguing the country's flora and fauna before this collection existed to hold it. It has sat inside Quinta Normal Park ever since, the oldest of the trio and still keeper of the natural-history record.
s: Founded in 1830 by a wandering French naturalist
_facts: one of three national museums in Chile, along with the Museum of Fine Arts and the National History Museum
located in Quinta Normal Park, founded in 1830 by French naturalist Claudio Gay
_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean National Museum of Natural History

w: Between 1974 and 1978, some 4,500 political prisoners passed through this DINA complex on the city's edge - at least 240 of them never came out. Its commander, Marcelo Moren Brito, was eventually convicted of crimes against humanity and handed a sentence north of 300 years, long after the torture rooms had gone quiet.
s: DINA's torture complex, now a site of memory
_facts: considered the most important of DINA's detention and torture complexes under Pinochet, operated mid-1974 to mid-1978 in Peñalolén
about 4,500 detainees brought there, at least 240 disappeared or were killed
headquarters of the Metropolitan Intelligence Brigade; head Marcelo Moren Brito was later convicted of crimes against humanity and sentenced to more than 300 years

w: Four earlier churches stood and fell on this site before construction finally settled in for the long haul - 1748 to 1906, spanning more than a century and outlasting several architects. Facing the Plaza de Armas, the finished cathedral now anchors an ensemble of national monuments, the fifth attempt finally sticking.
s: The fifth church raised on this exact spot
_facts: seat of the Archdiocese of Santiago, located facing the Plaza de Armas, dedicated to the Assumption of the Virgin Mary
built between 1748 and 1906, designed by Joaquín Toesca and Ignacio Cremonesi, the fifth temple built on the site
the architectural ensemble, including the Archbishop's Palace and Parish del Sagrario, are considered national monuments

w: Spanish conquistadors named this hill for Saint Christopher, patron of travelers, because it worked as a landmark long before street signs existed. Rising 300 metres above the city, it's still exactly that today - a navigational fixed point the Mapuche knew as Tupahue centuries before the Spanish ever climbed it.
s: Named by conquistadors, still Santiago's landmark
_facts: hill in northern Santiago rising 880 m AMSL and about 300 m above the rest of the city, third highest point in the city
named by Spanish conquistadors for St Christopher in recognition of its use as a landmark
original indigenous Mapuche name is Tupahue

n: Chilean National Museum of Fine Arts
w: The oldest art museum on the continent, founded in 1880 and rehoused in 1910 inside a Beaux-Arts palace built to mark Chile's independence centennial. Architect Emile Jequier gave it enough grandeur that the Museum of Contemporary Art simply moved in behind it - two collections sharing one Parque Forestal address.
s: South America's oldest art museum, since 1880
_facts: established in 1880, making it the oldest art museum in South America

current building, the Palace of the Fine Arts, dates to 1910, commemorating the centennial of Chilean independence, designed by architect Emile Jéquier in Beaux-Arts style, situated in Parque Forestal
the Museum of Contemporary Art of the University of Chile is located behind it
_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean National Museum of Fine Arts

w: Barely 69 metres above the surrounding streets, this outcrop known to the Mapuche as Huelen Hill got a full baroque makeover - ornate facades, stairways, and fountains packed into 65,300 square metres of park. Climb to the summit viewpoint and the whole absurdly theatrical design suddenly makes sense.
s: A tiny hill dressed up like a baroque folly
_facts: also known in Mapuche as Huelén Hill, altitude 629 m, height 69 m over the surrounding area
the hill comprises a 65,300 square metre park adorned with ornate facades, stairways and fountains
there is a viewpoint at the summit

w: Everybody in Santiago ends up here eventually: three major avenues and three parks converge on this oval plaza, built in 1928 over what used to be a fork in the Mapocho River. It is also the city's default stage for celebration and unrest alike - a championship party one week, a riot the next.
s: Where avenues, parks, and every riot converge
_facts: commonly known as Plaza Italia, inaugurated in 1928, crowned by a monument to General Manuel Baquedano
located where the Mapocho River used to fork; focal point of celebrations and riots in the city
hub of Santiago's street network where Providencia Avenue, Alameda, and Vicuña Mackenna Avenue intersect; Parque Forestal, Balmaceda Park and Bustamante Park converge here

w: Founded in 1852, decades before Chile's desert observatories made the country an astronomy powerhouse, this hilltop outpost in Las Condes has quietly watched the sky ever since - absorbed into the University of Chile in 1927 and rebuilt on Cerro Calan in 1962. A modest elder beside the country's giant telescopes.
s: 170-year-old stargazing outpost on a city hilltop
_facts: astronomical observatory owned and operated by the Department of Astronomy of the University of Chile, located on Cerro Calán in Las Condes
founded in 1852, became part of the University of Chile in 1927
the facility on Cerro Calán was completed in 1962

w: Since 2005 this museum has run as two separate operations across the city, one of them sharing a roof with the National Museum of Fine Arts inside the 1910 Palacio de Bellas Artes. Founded in 1947 under the University of Chile, its 2,000-plus pieces track modern art from well before 'contemporary' was a category.
s: One museum, two sites, one shared 1910 palace
_facts: created in 1947, run by the University of Chile Faculty of Arts
since 2005 has had two separate sites: MAC Parque Forestal and MAC Quinta Normal Park
collection made up of over 2,000 pieces; the Parque Forestal site shares the Palacio de Bellas Artes building with the National Museum of Fine Arts

w: Pablo Neruda built this house in 1953 for his secret lover Matilde Urrutia, naming it for her wild red hair - 'chascona' means tangled or disheveled. A 1955 Diego Rivera portrait hides Neruda's own profile woven into her curls, a coded declaration. Damaged in the 1973 coup, the house was later restored into a museum.
s: A secret lover's house, hiding a poet's face in her hair
_facts: house in Barrio Bellavista owned by Pablo Neruda, one of three houses associated with him
construction began 1953, initially intended as a residence for Matilde Urrutia, Neruda's secret lover at the time; name refers to her curly red hair
a 1955 Diego Rivera painting of Urrutia hides Neruda's profile concealed in her hair
the house sustained damage amid the 1973 military coup and was later restored, now functions as a museum

w: Santiago's grandest stage doubles as headquarters for the National Opera of Chile - reckoned the single most important theatre and opera house in the country. It has anchored the capital's performing arts scene for generations, still the address every touring production wants to play.
s: Home to the National Opera of Chile
_facts: the Teatro Municipal, National Opera of Chile, is the most important stage theatre and opera house in Santiago

w: Completed in 1989 in the Ñuñoa district, this modest building holds a simple distinction: it was the first mosque ever built in Chile. Its name, 'Mosque of Peace,' has anchored the country's Sunni Muslim community ever since - a first that took until the late twentieth century to arrive.
s: Chile's very first mosque, built in 1989
_facts: Sunni Muslim mosque located in Ñuñoa, meaning 'Mosque of Peace'
building completed in 1989, the first mosque in Chile

w: Planted in 1841 to grow foreign species in experimental greenhouses, this park hosted the Chilean International Exhibition of 1875 and now shelters sixteen historic steam locomotives in its railway museum. Even the water crane is an artifact: shipped from Bath, England, that same exhibition year, and still standing.
s: 16 steam engines parked inside a 19th-century park
_facts: urban park spanning 35.5 hectares, founded in 1841, originally intended for greenhouses to cultivate foreign plant species
hosted the Chilean International Exhibition in 1875
home to the Santiago Railway Museum displaying 16 historic steam locomotives; its water crane dates from 1875 and was built in England by Stothert & Pitt in Bath, Somerset

n: Basílica de Nuestra Señora del Perpetuo Socorro
w: Construction on this Gothic Revival church began in 1906, the year the Valparaiso earthquake forced engineers to rip up the plans and rebuild it stronger in reinforced concrete - unusually modern for a building this ornate. Belgian missionary priests designed it, and one of their own carved the sacristy door by hand.
s: Reinforced concrete Gothic, built through an earthquake
_facts: Latin Catholic Church designed in Gothic Revival style by Redemptorist priests Gustave Knockaert ('Brother Gerardo') and Huberto Boulangeot, foundation stone laid 12 December 1904
construction began in 1906, coinciding with the Valparaíso earthquake which caused plans to be modified for structural reinforcement
built with reinforced concrete planned by American engineer Juan Tonkin; Brother Joaquín Chardin carved the sacristy door and congregation's coat of arms
_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basílica de Nuestra Señora del Perpetuo Socorro

w: Behind the Neo-Renaissance facade of this basilica sits an unlikely museum piece: a rongorongo tablet from Easter Island, one of just twenty-nine such carved boards known to survive anywhere. The building dates to 1760, with towers added in 1859 and 1885 - a quiet Chilean National Monument hiding a Pacific mystery.
s: One of 29 surviving Easter Island tablets, in a church
_facts: founded by the Order of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mercy, third temple on site built in 1760, first tower built 1859, second tower 1885
a Chilean National Monument, Neo-Renaissance in architecture, with a small museum of religious objects and art
its collection includes pieces from Easter Island, including a rongorongo tablet, one of 29 left in the world

w: Planned in the 1930s in neo-Byzantine style, this basilica wraps its dome in sixteen carved prophets and floods the interior with 650 square metres of stained glass from the Gabriel Loire studio in France. A grotto out front lends its name to the nearby metro station - so commuters carry a little of Lourdes with them.
s: 650 square metres of stained glass, ringed by 16 prophets
_facts: church standing laterally opposite Quinta Normal Park, planned in the 1930s by architects Eduardo Costabal and Andrés Garafulic, built in neo-Byzantine style
features stained glass windows by Gabriel Loire Studio covering 650 square metres; base of the main dome ringed by 16 statues of prophets by sculptor Lily Garafulic
a Gruta de Lourdes faces the main facade, giving its name to the nearby Gruta de Lourdes metro station

w: Tucked underground beneath the Plaza de la Ciudadania, this cultural center sits behind the southern facade of the Palacio de La Moneda - Chile's government seat hiding an entire subterranean arts venue in its shadow. Built to put Santiago on the cultural circuit, it's as much architectural surprise as gallery space.
s: A cultural center buried beneath the presidential palace
_facts: cultural facility located under Plaza de la Ciudadanía, in the southern façade of the Palacio de La Moneda
intended to place Chile's capital in the international cultural circuit, allowing participative access to cultural and audiovisual richness
_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centro Cultural Palacio de La Moneda
